News.title: Labour urged to tackle crisis of jobless young people by cutting hiring costs
News.content:
LABOUR is being urged to tackle the crisis of jobless young people by cutting hiring costs.

Tax rises are making it hard for firms to employ them, according to MPs.





Higher minimum wages, National Insurance hikes and employment rights changes are hitting businesses.

The number of NEETs — young people not in education, employment or training — is close to a million.

Tory Shadow Chancellor Sir Mel Stride said: “Builders are desperate to hire [young people] but Labour have piled on costs that make it too expensive to give them a chance.

“You don’t fix youth unemployment by taxing the jobs they need. If we want our kids earning, we’ve got to cut the costs and stop pricing young people out of work.”

Reform’s Lee Anderson said: “All Labour has been successful at is destroying the job market while young people struggle to get a foot on the ladder.”

The Sun on Sunday’s Builder Better Britain campaign has helped secure youngsters placements in construction trades.

A Government spokesman said: “This Government inherited a dire shortage of construction workers and is determined to deliver more opportunities.

“That’s why our youth employment support package, totalling £2.5billion, includes the offer of £2,000 for each new employee aged 16 to 24 taken on by a small business, supporting almost one million young people and delivering up to 500,000 opportunities to earn and learn.”



They said those hiring under-21s earning below a certain level do not pay NI contributions.

News.title: Britain is at its weakest in 400 years – we need to prioritise bullets over benefits, Kemi Badenoch warns Starmer
News.content:
KEMI Badenoch has warned Britain is at its weakest in 400 years — as she pledged to go on the biggest ever peacetime rearming blitz.

The Tory leader said the UK has been “prioritising benefits over bullets” and is facing a day of reckoning.





Unleashing both ­barrels on PM Sir Keir Starmer, she branded his failure to find the billions needed to fund our military “a national disgrace”.

And she accused the Government of lying by ­pretending we are prepared for war, adding: “We are not ready.”

Ms Badenoch was speaking at the London Defence Conference, where she set out her plan to ramp up defence spending.

It came as the US and Iran held the first day of peace talks in Pakistan.



She said President Donald Trump had doled out some uncomfortable home truths — that Britain “cannot properly defend ourselves” without the US.

She said: “It is the culmination of long-standing policy failures which have left our defence capabilities arguably at their weakest in 400 years.

“I don’t need to tell you how this happened.

“Between 1989 and 2022, defence spending fell every year.



“We have grown fat on welfare. Prioritising benefits over bullets.”

The war in Iran exposed our shortcomings — with the UK unable to even send a warship to the region as missiles rained down on our allies and bases, she added.

Ms Badenoch said: “For a proud nation used to stamping its ­influence on the world, Britain’s lack of ­readiness for this war in Iran has been shocking.

“We weren’t just unprepared ­militarily, with no Royal Navy ­warships in the Middle East for the first time in decades. We were strategically unprepared too.”

Blame for this lies with the PM and not our brave Royal Navy, the Tory leader claimed.



She said Sir Keir has been too busy U-turning on benefits and caving to his rebellious backbenchers to prepare for war.

She said: “We have a Government that was politically unprepared for this war, distracted by its own infighting and psychodrama.

“The war in the Gulf must act as a wake-up call. Not for navel ­gazing or finger pointing about who did what, but for action.”

The Government-commissioned strategic defence review, co-authored by General Sir Richard Barrons, was published last year.

It set out the urgent rearming programme needed to make the UK war-ready.



But the Government has still not published the investment plan ­setting out how it will pay for higher defence spending.

Ms Badenoch branded this delay a “national scandal” and added: “Our Government literally doesn’t have a plan.”

Laying out her alternative defence spending blueprint, she promised to cut welfare and Net Zero projects to pay for weapons.

She said: “The next Conservative Government would reinstate the two-child benefit cap and spend that money on defence.

“That will fund the largest net increase in British troops under any Government since the Second World War. We will use the money to recruit 6,000 regular soldiers and 14,000 reservists — as well as paying for their accommodation and equipment.



“And we will reallocate £17billion from Government R&D [research and development work] and Ed Miliband’s disastrous Net Zero ­projects to create a new ­Sovereign Defence Fund.”

In a direct plea to the PM, she said the Tories will put party politics aside and unite with Labour to find cash for defence spending.

She said: “Let’s find the money to rearm. Let’s identify the ­spending cuts.

“And if we reach agreement on a joint plan, Conservatives will ­support those measures in ­Parliament on a three-line whip.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

But No10 hit out at the ­Conservative leader’s offer.



A Downing Street spokeswoman said: “Kemi Badenoch sat around the Cabinet table when the Conservatives hollowed-out our Armed Forces. We have announced the biggest uplift in defence spending since the Cold War

“We won’t be taking any advice from her.”

News.title: Construction industry is crying out for young labourers… but Govt policies have priced youngsters out of jobs
News.content:
Shameful waste of Britain’s young

IT IS a national disgrace that a million youngsters are sitting on the scrapheap.

Nearly 13 per cent of all 16 to 24-year-olds are not in education or employment.



What makes this disaster even worse is that the construction industry is crying out for young labourers.



The Government’s ludicrously ambitious target of building 1.5million new homes by 2029 already looks like falling short by as much as a third.

Building firms need a quarter of a million new workers, like the youngsters we took to sites across the UK this week to get work experience.

So why can’t bosses plug their own gap and take 250k youngsters off the dole at the same time?

Because of the Government’s own ruinous policies of course.

They have priced youngsters out of jobs and tied employers in knots of red tape.

Under Labour’s increased minimum wage, firms simply can’t afford to train young people and the apprentice scheme is a sprawling mess.

This double failure is shameful.

It lets down a generation of youngsters who want to work but are confined to welfare, some for the rest of their lives.



And it is blocking the vital housing programme Britain so desperately needs.

Sir Keir Starmer is keen to trumpet the importance of Labour values.

What value is there in allowing this shambles to continue?

How many chances?

ANYONE who thinks our broken justice system is a recent phenomenon should study the insane case of rapist Neil Trennan.

This monster was first jailed for life in 1990 when he raped a woman after attacking her with a dumb-bell.



Yet in 2002 he was allowed day release, escaped from his supervisor and launched a sexually motivated attack on another woman, receiving a second life sentence.

In any normal system that would be enough to prevent him ever receiving leniency again.

But not in the opinion of the Parole Board, who recommended him for an open prison in 2023.

Astonishingly this fiend, who admitted he was addicted to sexual violence, was then allowed out on unsupervised day release, during which he absconded and tried to rape a third woman.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The judge who handed him a third life sentence in February is absolutely right to demand Justice Secretary David Lammy immediately investigate this outrage.



Mr Lammy must identify those responsible for letting this sex beast roam free and kick them out of the justice system.

News.title: Cruel words about late Queen are shameful and unnecessary – but evil specimen Andrew has made her an easy target
News.content:
IT is less than four years since the longest-reigning monarch in British history died.

But how quickly memories fade.





During that short time, some have forgotten all the good Queen Elizabeth II did during her 70 years on the throne.

They are also overlooking the respect she still deserves.

A new profile on her has been written in the (once!) respected Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, which is supposed to serve as a record of our notable public figures.

But it resembles something your average Gen Zer would put on TikTok.

It says the UK “ceased to be a great power in the world” under her.

It claims she adapted “slowly and not always enthusiastically” as Britain evolved into “a multicultural, multi-faith, multi-ethnic society”.

The biased anti-royalists wrote that she “had not been born to succeed” but by her “example, her self-discipline, her public spiritedness, and her longevity, she did so in more ways than one, living out perhaps the most remarkable life of her times.”

It makes her sound like a bigoted old aunt, forced into a job she didn’t want, but we just kind of tolerated her because she stuck around for so long.





This couldn’t be further from the truth. She was respected, loved and admired.

So many of the words seem cruel and unnecessary.

They have also chastised her “mis-steps” (particularly in relation to her family). And maybe here lies the real problem: Andrew.

Because of this vile specimen, who denies any wrongdoing, she has become an easy target. But just like us, the Queen didn’t know the truth before her death.

You don’t have to like the monarch to write about her.

But if you’re compiling her national biography profile, you should really make it your business to know what her role entailed.

A constitutional monarch serves as the ceremonial head of state.

Yes, the Prime Minister consults the monarch — and she would encourage and warn — but she didn’t make the political decisions that shape this country.

She graciously, invisibly, guided 15 Prime Ministers from the wings. (And how unsteady things have come without her presence.) This stabilising figure also urged, over many decades, people to embrace diversity, cultures, faiths and the Commonwealth.

As her job was to guide, not to tell us what to do, I am not quite sure how “enthusiastic” the authors of this barbed biography expected her to be.



Sense of duty

Her work was tireless, with 21,000 royal engagements in all.

She made friends along the way, from Nelson Mandela to comedian Billy Connolly, and showed her own great sense of humour in sketches with James Bond for the Olympic Games, with Paddington for her Jubilee.

She supported grandson Harry’s Invictus Games.

During Covid she remained strong and stabilising, telling us: “We will be with our friends again; we will be with our families again; we will meet again.”

She always led by example, always had a sense of duty.

Even at her husband’s funeral, when she sat alone to adhere to Covid distancing regulations.

We will never forget that haunting image of her with a black mask covering her pale face and just those glistening eyes visible above.

Our hearts went out to the nation’s grandmother and we wanted to console her.

Now is our chance to support her again.

Because so many of us do.



Half the country watched her funeral when she died.

And this month, as we celebrate what would have been her 100th birthday, let’s all pay our respects again.

Spread the positive truth about this great monarch to our own grandchildren so they hear about her from us, not that shameful biography.

We must cherish her great memory, not desecrate it.

I’M LOVING ANGEL’S EVERLASTING LOOK

THERE was a time when your granny looked, well, old. But how times have changed.

When Kate Jackson, Jaclyn Smith and Cheryl Ladd celebrated 50 years of TV show Charlie’s Angels this week, they could have passed for women decades younger. Especially Jaclyn.

She’s 80 and old enough to be my mother but could easily pass as my sister.

She maintains her ageless looks with a healthy lifestyle and diet, a good skin care routine and perhaps the key is that she uses her “own fat” for facial enhancement.



If that’s all it takes, lucky her. I’m all for a few tweakments when my credit card allows.

Now Jaclyn has become a pensioner influencer, other women might also want to hurtle towards an aesthetics clinic after collecting their bus pass.

But there’s only so much nipping and pricking you can do without looking ridiculous.

And Jaclyn has something most of us have never had – natural supermodel beauty, with flawless skin and cheekbones to die for.

She wouldn’t have got to say “Good morning” to Charlie for five years without those genes.

GROW UP, YOU BRATS

WHAT a disappointing pair of brats Sydney Sweeney and Zendaya have turned into.

They were once firm friends but Sydney is said to have flirted with Zendaya’s “is-he-isn’t-he-hubby” Tom Holland and they are also suffering from some sort of career rivalry.

But their career is acting – their current job is promoting their raunchy show Euphoria, and putting on a red-carpet performance is part of the job description.



Maybe they should have remembered that and acted like professional grown-ups, rather than refusing to even stand on it together at the premiere.

lTHERE is a strange new illness spreading around the pet world.

A study in the Netherlands has found that cat and dog owners are making false claims that their animals are sick – or even harming them – to seek attention from vets.

The majority of clinics there are familiar with the phenomenon.

The RSPCA says it’s also happening here despite huge vet bills.

These people have more money than sense.

READY, OR NOT

I’VE started a new health kick and it’s all thanks to Watford businessman Stephen Akuoko.

After reading about how he kept fish in a bath next his toilet before cooking them into ready-meals, I’ve gone right off convenience food.



All meals will now be cooked from scratch.

EGG ON THEIR FACES

IF you’ve been asked to look after something important by your boss that’s, say, priceless or even a collector’s piece, or for example a Faberge egg and watch set valued at up to £2.2million, what would you do with them to keep them safe?

A) Put them in an actual safe.

B) Keep them under your pillow.

C) Shove them in your bag and pop to the packed Dog and Duck pub in London’s Soho.

Oddly, Rosie Dawson opted for C.

Rosie was supposed to be guarding the Faberge items after taking them for display at a work event for her employers at the Craft Irish Whiskey Company.

But in the pub she put the bag down to greet a friend and quick-thinking thief Enzo Conticello swiped it – and its high-value goodies.



He flogged the lot to buy drugs and has been jailed for 27 months.

During his sentence he was told the theft had caused “inconvenience and stress” to Rosie and her company.

I imagine they all needed a stiff drink to get over that loss.

CHOC & CAW

STARS seemed to align last Sunday.

The weather in Manchester was good, I didn’t hit snooze on the 5.30am alarm, and hid chocolate all over my garden.

But 90 minutes later, when my seven-year-old went out with his basket, many of the foil-wrapped chocolate figures had disappeared.

It took a hunt of my own on our security camera to find the culprit . . . a great big thieving magpie.

Hope he was sick.

WHEN Greek prime minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis announced he was banning social media for teens to tackle anxiety and sleep problems, he added that “many of the younger ones among you will be angry with me”.

Now, yes, but they will thank him one day.

News.title: Sadiq Khan has to wake up… horror on Primrose Hill shows London I love is teetering on the edge of lawlessness
News.content:
IF Britain was not stark raving mad, we’d be honouring Walker Smith today.

Mr Smith, 54, tackled a shoplifter in Waitrose, his place of work for the last 17 years.





The man should have got a medal. Instead, he got the sack.

Because when Walker Smith saw some lowlife stuffing her bag with multiple Lindt Gold Bunny Easter eggs that she had not paid for, he intervened.

“I’ve seen it happen every hour of every day for the last five years,” he said.

“It’s everybody, from drug addicts to teenagers, nicking bits and bobs or walking out with bottles of wine in their arms. We’re not allowed to do anything.”

The cops, the courts and our political masters do not give a toss about shoplifting. But Walker Smith cared.

And caring cost this principled, decent man his job.

I have seen Mr Smith described as a security guard but that is incorrect. Walker was a shop assistant.

Security had been scaled back — “Because shoplifting incidents aren’t reported enough” — leaving non-security staff like Walker on the front line of the shoplifting plague.





So how can his employer imagine that he is the bad guy?

“There is a serious danger to life in tackling shoplifters,” simpered a witless Waitrose spokesperson.

“And that’s why we have policies in place that must be strictly followed.”

In other words — let the thieving bastards get away with it.

And Sir Sadiq Khan, Labour Mayor of London, has the brass neck to insist that the capital is “a safe city”.

Sadiq’s unconvincing evidence?

The cold comfort of knowing that London has a lower murder rate than “every state in the USA”.

As if having a lower homicide rate than gun-mad, psycho-stuffed America was a reason to break out the bubbly.

“Unfortunately, London-bashing has become something of a national and international sport with populist politicians, commentators and keyboard warriors trading in fear, not facts,” sighed Sadiq.

“We should be proud of how safe London is,” echoes Sir Mark Rowley, Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police.



But in the first few weeks of spring, horrific crimes have occurred all over the capital.

On Primrose Hill during a sunny afternoon, a 21-year-old man was stabbed to death.

Finbar Sullivan had taken his new camera — a 21st birthday present — to Primrose Hill to take some photographs. Finbar never came home.

Here was a gentle, creative young man who did his best to steer clear of trouble.

“When he got a scooter, he would ride to school and it would take him ages because he would avoid all the areas where there were gangs,” said Finbar’s heartbroken father, Chris Sullivan.

“He did not wear black because of that — he didn’t want to be associated with any gangs. He wore pale colours.”

Finbar knew all the dangers. It did not save him.

Just five days earlier, Eghosa Ogbebor was shot dead in Woolwich — another murder in broad daylight. Eghosa was 14.

In Golders Green, Jewish ambulances were firebombed.

And in Clapham, a mob of youths ran riot, ransacking shops and terrifying families.



And there is one reason for this social breakdown. There are far too many scumbags out there who believe that they are going to get away with their crime.

From shoplifting to carrying — and using — a deadly weapon.

From stealing Easter eggs to stealing phones to stealing some innocent boy’s life.

Running riot

Behind every single one of these crimes I guarantee that there is someone who thinks that they will never be punished.

Take your head out of the sand, Mr Mayor. Wake up and smell the sewer that our beloved London is becoming, Sir Mark.

This week the Met showed off its new fleet of armoured vehicles, £180,000 nine-tonne monsters called SandCats.

The money would have been better spent putting more old-school coppers on the street.

Because we desperately need a mayor who can see the heart-wrenching reality of crime running riot in the capital. We need cops who care, laws that bite, courts that are capable of making the scumbags fear that they will be punished.

The London I love is teetering on the edge of total lawlessness.



Sacked by Waitrose, Walker Smith has been offered a job by Lord Richard Walker, the boss of Iceland.

Lord Walker wants security guards to carry truncheons and pepper spray to fight shoplifting — that cosy euphemism for retail theft.

In Sainsbury’s, some security guards have been issued stab vests.

Costa Coffee has started having bouncers on the door across the capital to guard fridges.

Stab vests in Sainsbury’s! Bouncers in coffee shops!

There is not one worker in a London supermarket who does not feel that they are in mortal danger every day they go to work.

And Sadiq Khan complacently assures us London is a safe city?

Mr Mayor, you are out of your tiny mind.

Sydney to join the Q

HOLLYWOOD director Paul Feig suggests Sydney Sweeney should be the next James Bond.



“There have been some cool Bond girls,” says Paul, who directed El Syd in domestic thriller The Housemaid. “But come on! Let her be the super-spy. She’s great.”

Seems a bit of a long shot. But when Sweeney was once asked if she fancied being a Bond girl, she retorted: “I think I would have more fun as James Bond.”

She was not kidding. The Housemaid was shot for a reported $35million and has made about $399 million worldwide.

Which makes Sweeney the hottest star in Tinseltown. Could she really be the next 007?

With those kinds of figures at the box office, Sydney Sweeney can be whatever she likes.

WHEN they flew around the far side of the moon, the astronauts on Artemis II ventured deeper into space than anyone has ever been – 252,760 miles from Planet Earth.

An extraordinary moment for humanity.

And despite the calm, smiling competence of the crew, they were putting their lives at risk for every second.

The most memorable moment of my childhood was gazing up at the moon in the summer of 1969 and knowing that humans were walking on its surface. Isn’t it glorious to be back?

Trump fuels EU fans



THERE is a theory that Donald Trump is driving the UK back into the arms of the European Union. You can see the logic.

Most of us do not mind if the POTUS is rude about our socialist Prime Minister. We can’t stand him either.

But all of us feel our blood boil when the President is abusive about British Armed Forces.

In January Trump sneered that in Afghanistan – where the UK had 457 military deaths and thousands of our brave men and women suffered life- changing injuries – frightened Nato troops stayed “a little off the front line”.

Trump quickly retracted that lie. But his sneering has never really stopped. This President is too quick to casually call us cowards.

And disgustingly chummy with Russia’s Vladimir Putin.

A YouGov poll revealed that only 14 per cent of British people still believe we have a “special relationship” with America, 57 per cent want to get closer to the EU.

And if the European Union was smart, it would be wooing this country, and welcoming us back with open arms.

But it is not smart.

Watch the appetite for Rejoining shrivel when we contemplate the real cost. Finally giving up the pound for the euro.



Throwing open our borders and learning to love the Schengen Area.

Forgetting about the budget rebate negotiated by Margaret Thatcher.

And above all, bitterly regretting the error of our Brexit-voting ways and begging Europe for forgiveness.

This is what will stop us ever going back inside the EU. Brussels will want us to crawl.

Cheers Philip A NEW book, Queen Elizabeth II, by Hugo Vickers, describes in vivid detail the last night of Prince Philip’s life. Vickers reports that Philip “gave his nurses the slip, shuffled along the corridor on his Zimmer frame and helped himself to a beer”. The next morning the Duke quietly slipped away after a bath. He was 99 years old. That’s the way to go.

JOANNA LUMLEY, 79, joined a neighbour in confronting a gang of bikers attempting to steal her car from outside her home in Stockwell, South London.

The gang fled empty-handed when they saw the glint in Joanna’s eyes.

Which is possibly a bit of a surprise if you only know Lumley as pie-eye fashionista Patsy in Absolutely Fabulous.

But if you first saw her as karate-chopping, butt-kicking Purdey in The New Avengers, then it was totally in character.

I bet pet soon Fritz in with Heidi’s hubby

HEIDI KLUM steps out in New York with a mystery companion – a Yorkshire terrier mix called Fritz, who is from a pop-up adoption centre next to where the model and TV host was working.



“It took some convincing with my husband,” confesses Heidi.

Heidi’s husband will come around.

It is always the family member who is most resistant to the idea of getting a dog who falls most deeply in love with his new four-legged roommate.

News.title: How cut-price ‘direct cremations’ could lead to MORE monster funeral directors giving families wrong ashes
News.content:
FEARS are growing that cut-price “direct cremations” could encourage monsters like rogue funeral director Robert Bush.

One in five funerals now takes place without a service or mourners, with the ashes simply posted back to the grieving family.





After the horrific scandal of funeral director Bush, who this month pleaded guilty to giving families the wrong ashes and leaving bodies in his parlour for months, we can reveal there are fears rogue funeral directors could be disposing of bodies by putting two in a coffin to avoid paying cremation fees.

Rosie Inman-Cook, from charity The Natural Death Centre, says the unregulated industry is currently a “wild west of cowboys” who need no licence or qualifications to set up a funeral parlour.

‘Wild west of cowboys’

She said: “There’s nothing to stop any funeral director potentially putting two bodies in a coffin and cremating them together. The only way to prevent it is to legislate that when a coffin arrives at any cemetery, the lid has to be removed for the contents to be checked.

“This problem increases with direct cremation because there is no family there. And more and more people are choosing these.

“It’s a third of the cost of a regular cremation so families who are hard up are choosing that option.

“Some funeral directors tell ­relatives they are doing a cremation, but they don’t book it in and it doesn’t happen. They are given any old ash in a box, and told it is their loved one. Vulnerable people are being preyed upon.

“When a coffin arrives at a cemetery you trust the funeral director is being honest. They don’t take the lid off and look inside.

“If a family saw their tiny granny’s ­coffin and it’s 7ft foot long with six huffing and puffing pall bearers, they would suspect, but there’s a risk it could go unnoticed.





“Because there is no regulation, there’s nothing to stop gangsters and criminals setting up a funeral directors and disposing of people that way.”

Direct cremations can cost as little as £1,000 compared with £3,500 to £4,000 for a full ceremony, and are heavily advertised on TV and radio to the elderly as a low-cost way to avoid burdening loved ones with expensive funeral costs.

They represented 21 per cent of UK funerals last year, up from three per cent in 2019, according to a report from the insurer Sunlife.

As well as cost, the effect of the pandemic – when social distancing rules limited the number of people who could attend a service – has made them more common.

Adherence to a mandatory code of practice and licensing is law in Scotland under the Burial And Cremation Act 2016.

Funeral directors there are subject to mandatory, legally enforced regulations.

There are also strict requirements on washing, dressing and maintaining the dignity of the deceased, and inspections of facilities.

In England and Wales there are only voluntary schemes provided by trade bodies including the National Association of Funeral Directors, which has seen complaints more than double in the past three years from 231 in 2021/22 to 470 in 2024/25.



Bush, 47, gave relatives the wrong ashes while their loved ones’ bodies were left in his parlour for months.

Officers found 35 corpses and more than 100 sets of ashes at Legacy Independent Funeral Directors, in Hull, in March 2024.

One of the bodies had been there for a year.

After a guilty plea he will be sentenced in July.

Sets of ashes

In February, funeral directors ­Richard Elkin, and Hayley Bell were jailed for four years at Portsmouth Crown Court after leaving 46 bodies to decompose in a warm mortuary for more than a month, and ­were convicted of intentionally causing a public nuisance, preventing lawful burial, and carrying on business with intent to defraud creditors.

In January, undertaker Jack Weekes was convicted in Cornwall after keeping the body of an 86-year-old woman for more than a month after he should have cremated her.

He got 15 months, suspended for two years.

Michaela Baldwin’s stepdad was one of the victims involved in the Legacy Independent Funeral Directors case.

When she went there to say her last goodbye to stepdad Danny Middleton, she couldn’t help but notice the size of his coffin.

The former delivery driver, who was fond of ­Sunday roast dinners, had been a large man when he died in his 70s after long-term ill health relating to his heart.



Michaela, 35, a full-time mum, said: “When I saw the coffin I thought, ‘There is no way Danny can be in that’, but you are grieving. You think, ‘They’re the ­specialists, they know what they are doing’. He’s got to be in there. You only hear of that kind of stuff in horror films.”

The family had paid for a cremation, and were later given some ashes, which Danny’s nieces had been planning to turn into jewellery.

But in March 2024 Humberside Police revealed they were investigating the undertakers and the family got in touch.

They learned Danny’s body was still at the premises.

She says: “Danny ­was a wonderful man. He didn’t deserve this.

“When I eventually found out the truth, all I could think was, ‘Who the hell have we got? Who is this poor soul?’ We will never know.”



Funeral company Plan With Grace was recently fined because they posted ashes back to the wrong ­country.

A daughter, known as Mrs R, lodged the complaint with the financial ombudsman, after paying £1,440 for a direct cremation for her mother in 2024.

Her ashes were wrongly sent to an unnamed EU country.

By the time they arrived, there was “spillage and loss”.

The company tried to blame Royal Mail but the ombudsman ordered Plan With Grace to repay £1,000.

Rupert Callender, who runs the Green Funeral Company in Dartington, Devon, says hospitals are ­complaining about direct funerals, too.

He said: “A lot of the larger, more impersonal companies keep bodies in huge body hubs like some sort of grizzly Amazon warehouse.

“That disconnect means ­mistakes are bound to happen. Instead of undertakers, they have a guy with a van who drives around the hospitals collecting remains.

“Hospitals are exasperated because they’ve had to store bodies for weeks because direct companies have sold the family a funeral but not bothered to collect the body.”

Michaela is now campaigning for regulation and for “mandatory coffin inspections”.

News.title: Crypto-hunting gang hold terrified family at knifepoint and demand ‘key to millions’ in horror home invasion
News.content:
A WEALTHY businessman and his family were held at knifepoint in their home in a cryptocurrency robbery.

Oliver von Landsberg-Sadie, who founded leading London crypto firm the BCB Group, said the raiders demanded the keycode to his electronic wallet.





Stood next to an Aston Martin on his driveway, he told The Sun on Sunday: “They were only after crypto. They had no interest in my car.”

Oliver, 47, now chief of Greater Things, a multi-million-pound business using AI to launch tech firms, said four villains broke into his house in Maidenhead, Berks, and tied up him, wife Sarah and their two children.

South African Oliver said they were still shaken from their 10pm ordeal on April 2.

But he does not personally keep the digital money so the gang left disappointed.

However, they did nick cash, watches, and silver.

The day after, he warned other crypto tycoons online: “I was robbed at home at knifepoint last night, with my family, by four men looking for crypto specifically.

“There is clearly an organised campaign and I ask you to be more vigilant with your personal safety.”

He said: “It’s the sort of thing you see in the movies and never think will happen to you.



“They had no interest in the car, for example, because that’s traceable.

“Crypto is of course not the only thing burglars target but it’s true that it can be as vulnerable to theft as cash or jewellery if not kept securely.

“We live in a pretty safe country here but I’m from South Africa and nothing like this ever happened to me there.”

Thames Valley Police are hunting the culprits.

News.title: Person rushed to hospital after car smashes through window of Japanese restaurant
News.content:
DINER SCARE Person rushed to hospital after car smashes through window of Japanese restaurant

A PERSON is fighting for their life in hospital after a car ploughed into a Japanese restaurant in a town centre.

The Ford Kuga mounted the pavement and crashed into the window of the eatery in Wigston, Leicestershire.



Police, paramedics and fire crews all scrambled to Shokudo restaurant on Bell street just after 4pm today.



Leicestershire Police said one person in the building was rushed to hospital with “non-life threatening injuries”.

The driver and passenger of the car, a man and a woman both in their 80s, were unharmed in the crash.

One eye-witness told Leicestershire Live how they heard a loud bang while walking away from the restaurant.

“There’s extensive damage to the sushi shop.”

There have been no arrests in connection with the crash the force said.

A spokesperson added: “Officers are carrying out enquiries to ascertain the circumstances of the collision”.

They said: “Officers were called to the scene at 4.07pm this afternoon where a car – a Ford Kuga – has mounted the kerb and collided with a building.

“One person, who was inside the building, has been taken to hospital with non-life threatening injuries. Two people – a man and a woman in their 80s – who were inside the car were not injured.



“No arrests have been made.

“Officers remain at the scene and in the immediate area carrying out enquiries to ascertain the circumstances of the collision, including CCTV checks.”

Officers have urged anyone with information to call the force on 101.

News.title: Girl, 12, 'still can't speak' after teen used ChatGPT to plan horror school shooting
News.content:
Girl, 12, 'still can't speak' after teen used ChatGPT to plan horror school shooting

WARNING: DISTRESSING CONTENT Maya Gebala was shot three times during the rampage in British Columbia and still cannot speak or see two months after the horror incident

View 3 Images Maya Gebala, 12, is ‘fighting for her life’ after the Canadian school shooting (Image: GoFundMe)

A 12-year-old girl who was shot in the head during a school shooting in Canada remains unable to speak or see two months on from the horror incident.

‌



On February 10 the shooting claimed the lives of five innocent pupils and a teacher, leaving several others fighting for survival. The parents of 12-year-old Maya Gebala, aged 12, along with Bob Zimmer, a Member of the House of Commons of Canada, are working to pursue legal action against ChatGPT's parent company, OpenAI, as the perpetrator had been using the platform to assist in planning the shooting, and the service failed to notify the authorities.

‌



Jesse Van Rootselaar, 18, murdered their mother and half-brother before opening fire at the secondary school in a remote north-eastern corner of British Columbia. Van Rootselaar subsequently took their own life. It proved to be one of the deadliest shootings in Canadian history.

‌



View 3 Images Maya's mother Cia Edmonds shared this photo from hospital as she prayed for a miracle after doctors told her the little girl wouldn't last the night (Image: Facebook)

Parents' heartbreaking tribute to brave teen who died after leukaemia battle READ MORE :

Gebala, who remains hospitalised more than two months on, was shot three times — one bullet passing through her head above her left eye, another entering her neck, and a third grazing her cheek and part of her ear, according to the lawsuit. She is suffering from catastrophic traumatic brain injury, permanent cognitive and physical disability, right-sided hemiplegia, scarring, and physical deformities, reports the Mirror US.

She is reported to have been attempting to shield her classmates by trying to lock the doors to the school library to prevent the shooter from gaining entry. The victim's family and political figures are demanding answers, questioning whether the tragedy could have been prevented with earlier action. Zimmer told the Sun, "There were so many red flags and so many preventative things that could have been done to prevent the tragedy." He remains determined to help Gebala's family and all other victims obtain justice. "We will leave no stone unturned."

‌



OpenAI suspended an initial ChatGPT account used by the 18 year old suspect in June 2025 due to the deeply concerning nature of their conversations with the chatbot; however, Canadian police were never notified of the ban.

The lawsuit alleges that Van Rootselaar created a ChatGPT account before reaching the age of 18, which requires parental consent, but claims the platform failed to verify their age. The suit further states that Van Rootselaar confided in the chatbot, treating it as a "trusted confidante," and detailed "various scenarios involving gun violence" to it over multiple days in late spring or early summer of the previous year.

View 3 Images Flowers sit outside of Tumbler Ridge Secondary School where a shooting took place (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Article continues below

Twelve OpenAI employees reportedly flagged the conversations as "indicating an imminent risk of serious harm to others" and recommended that Canadian law enforcement be contacted to investigate, yet they never were.

However, the lawsuit alleges Van Rootselaar subsequently opened a second ChatGPT account despite the ban, which allowed them to "continue planning scenarios involving gun violence." OpenAI informed the BBC that it is committed to making "meaningful changes" to help avoid similar tragedies occurring in the future.

Gebala is reportedly in a stable condition and on his way to Los Angeles for specialist treatment.

News.title: NHS GP’s ‘weird’ ways to ditch hay fever including little-known ‘vaseline trick’
News.content:
NHS GP’s ‘weird’ ways to ditch hay fever including little-known ‘vaseline trick’

The expert shared some hay fever solutions that don’t involve medications

View 2 Images Millions of people in the UK suffer from hayfever (Image: GETTY)

Hay fever affects around 16 million people in the UK, many of which have likely experienced the first of their annual springtime symptoms as the Met Office issued a red alert for nine areas earlier this week and more pollen highs are expected as the season continues.

‌



An NHS GP is urging hay fever sufferers to add some different tools to their bag of treatments this year alongside the antihistamines and nasal sprays. Dr Asimah Hanif explained some stranger tricks and hacks that can help keep the spring allergens at bay even when you have to be venturing outside.

‌



Smear vaseline around your nose

The GP explained: “It's a simple barrier method, but it can be surprisingly effective, especially if you're heading outside on a high-pollen day. The NHS recommends it for a reason.

‌



“Just apply a small amount to the rim of each nostril before going out, and wipe and reapply when you come back in."

This thin layer can physically trap pollen and other airborne allergens before it gets a chance to enter your airways and cause a reaction. Some pharmacies may even offer dedicated allergy barrier balms if you don’t want to use Vaseline.

Gastroenterologist says rule of 'three' can add years to your life READ MORE :

Brits doing spring clean issued urgent 'toxic' warning for these cleaning products READ MORE :

Quercetin

Red onions, capers, apples and berries are some of the foods with high levels of quercetin. This is a plant flavonoid that has been shown to inhibit the release of histamine within your body, which is what causes hay fever symptoms.

‌



Dr Asimah said: "Quercetin works a bit like a natural antihistamine. It doesn't act as quickly as medication, and the evidence is stronger in lab settings than in clinical trials, but there's a real biological reason why people who eat a diet rich in these foods might find their symptoms more manageable. If you're already reaching for onions and berries regularly, keep it up."

Avoid smoke

Spring can see the resurgence in barbecues, fire pits and smoking areas but the doctor urged people with particularly bad hay fever symptoms to try avoid these areas. Smoke can irritate the nasal passages, which can be a miserable combination if you’re already dealing with pollen irritation.

She warned: "Smoke makes it harder for your airways to cope with pollen. It doesn't cause hay fever, but it significantly lowers your threshold for symptoms. On high-pollen days especially, it's worth giving bonfires and barbecues a wide berth."

‌



View 2 Images Red onions can be a natural antihistamine (Image: GETTY)

Check before you book

Some people may be heading abroad during the hay fever season in a bid to escape their symptoms but Dr Asimah, who works as a medical expert for travel insurance provider Staysure, warned it may worsen your situation.

Different countries have different pollen profiles, with some areas like Reykjavik having low year-round pollen counts while summer favourites like Madrid, Milan and Zurich having high levels particularly in the early summer months.

‌



Dr Asimah warned:. "It's not just about pollen levels, you're also being exposed to plant species you've never encountered before, so your immune system hasn't built any tolerance at all.

“Checking pollen forecasts for your destination before you travel is a really sensible step. People are sometimes surprised to find their symptoms are worse on holiday than at home.”

Hay fever, like any medical condition, should be declared to your travel insurer when you’re heading abroad but it likely won’t cause a price increase unless you also have asthma. The doctor urged: "If hay fever is affecting your asthma, making symptoms more frequent or harder to control you’ll want to know that you have the back up of you travel insurance just in case.

Article continues below

"Medical travel insurance exists precisely for situations like this, and not declaring the conditions you live with and manage on a daily basis can make an enormous difference if you need medical treatment for a flair up while you’re away or if something else goes wrong that could be related to one of the conditions.”

News.title: Trump 'struggles to close umbrella' as viral video sparks health concerns again
News.content:
Trump 'struggles to close umbrella' as viral video sparks health concerns again

Donald Trump was filmed throwing an umbrella to one side as he boarded Air Force One in another viral moment, with many questioning the President's actions.

View 2 Images Donald Trump struggles with umbrella (Image: SKY)

Donald Trump once again appeared to struggle with closing an umbrella, in yet another moment that has taken the internet by storm.

‌



The episode took place on Friday afternoon as he boarded Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, heading to his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida.

‌



Trump made his way up the steps towards the aircraft beneath stormy skies, but as he neared the plane's entrance, he appeared unable to fold his umbrella shut.

‌



The US President chose to abandon the umbrella altogether, tossing it aside before stepping into the cabin — just as he had done previously back in October.

The moment quickly went viral, with countless people questioning why he was unable to close it himself.

View 2 Images Trump gave up with the umbrella (Image: SKY)

‌



One wrote: "Even in small, insignificant gestures, Trump impressively demonstrates just what an idiot he is. He isn't even capable of closing an umbrella and leaves that to the Secret Service."

Another said: " Donald Trump is getting mocked after video shows him walking away without even closing his own umbrella before boarding the plane."

A third added: "Trump leaving the umbrella for someone else to close, because he can't do it himself, is a perfect illustration of what he did with Iran."

‌



And a fourth commented: "Classic Trump: he couldn't close the umbrella himself, so he just left it for someone else to deal with. Exactly what he did with Iran."

Negotiations have pressed on over the weekend between the US and Iran in Pakistan, several days after a fragile, two-week ceasefire was declared. The White House confirmed the direct nature of the talks, describing it as a rare instance of high-level engagement. Iranian state TV reported that negotiations were still ongoing as of 1am on Sunday in Islamabad.

Donald Trump has declared that the US has started clearing mines in the Strait of Hormuz "as a favor to countries all over the world".

Article continues below

In a post on his Truth Social app, the US president stated that Iran's minelaying vessels "are also lying at the bottom of the sea".

He further added: "The only thing they have going is the threat that a ship may 'bunk' into one of their sea mines which, by the way, all 28 of their mine dropper boats are also lying at the bottom of the sea.

"We're now starting the process of clearing out the Strait of Hormuz as a favour to Countries all over the World, including China, Japan, South Korea, France, Germany, and many others. Incredibly, they don't have the Courage or Will to do this work themselves."

News.title: Parents' heartbreaking tribute to brave teen who died after leukaemia battle
News.content:
Parents' heartbreaking tribute to brave teen who died after leukaemia battle

Grace Measor, 19, died on Friday, due to complications following a stem cell transplant. She had written letters to her family and friends to be opened in the event of her death, urging them to live their lives to the fullest

View 4 Images Grace Measor who tragically lost her battle on Friday (Image: Family handout)

The devastated parents of a Hartlepool teenager who lost her courageous battle with leukaemia have described her as "a gift to the world."

‌



Grace Measor passed away on Friday as a result of complications following a stem cell transplant. The kind-hearted 19 year old had penned letters to her loved ones to be opened upon her death, encouraging them to embrace life to the fullest and reassuring them "it's okay". The letters are bringing enormous comfort to dad Graeme, mum Nichola and sister Sophie, 17, as they struggle to come to terms with their heartbreaking loss.

‌



Diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia in 2017, Grace's initial treatment proved successful and she went on to excel at school, college and university before embarking on a career as a scientist with Johnson Mathey. Graeme and Nichola revealed she had dreamed of travelling the world and pursuing a career in research and development into renewables.

‌



View 4 Images Grace loved to travel and had wanted to make the world a better place (Image: Family handout)

"Basically she wanted to save the planet," said mum Nichola, 51, an occupational therapy care assistant. Graeme, who works as a senior lecturer at Teesside University, said they watched her flourish into "an absolutely amazing woman" after previously conquering the leukaemia.

"As parents, we decided at that point, that she had earned the right to do anything she wants," he said. "She got a travel bug and wanted to go places and if we could possibly make it happen we said yes and I'm glad we did." Grace's travels took her to Nepal, Turkey, Florida, Spain, Austria and France. "We took the opportunities when they arose - we made memories not material things," Nichola explained, reports Teesside Live.

‌



"Grace managed to make friends and collect people everywhere she goes. She is just loved in all directions, whether it was at school, college or work."

Grace was a pupil at Seaton Holy Trinity Primary School and Dyke House Academy in Hartlepool before continuing her studies at Middlesbrough College, then securing a degree apprenticeship at Manchester Metropolitan University. While at college, she entered a chemistry competition and reached the national finals in Cardiff.

View 4 Images A treasured family picture of Grace (Image: Family handout)

‌



However, on her journey to the contest, she started experiencing excruciating back pain. Following multiple hospital visits and examinations, her parents took her to the RVI in Newcastle in December, where a blood film confirmed their worst fears - her leukaemia had come back.

"The consultant said, 'you will have to go to the Freeman Hospital for a stem cell transplant,'" Graeme, 52, recalled. "She was told the treatment for the bone marrow transplant was total body radiation, followed by really strong chemotherapy to kill the bone marrow and then you get the stem cells which is an infusion.

"She was told it would make her sterile so, in order to preserve her fertility, she was brave enough, prior to coming in, to go to the RVI and have one of her ovaries harvested and frozen so that in the future she could have babies. At 19 to make that decision - her heroism was just unbelievable."

‌



After the treatment, Grace developed a chest infection and rare complications which struck her body simultaneously. This resulted in a catastrophic brain injury with no prospect of recovery, and the heartbreaking decision was taken by doctors to withdraw treatment. Grace passed away in the arms of her devoted parents and sister. She had penned letters to her family and friends to be opened if she didn't survive treatment.

View 4 Images The sisters were very close and Sophie held Grace as she passed away (Image: Family handout)

"They are full of so much maturity for somebody so young and they are giving us so much comfort," said Graeme. "One of the lines says: 'When you walk the dog along the seafront, I'm in the roaring of the ocean, I'm in the air that you breathe, I'm at one with nature, and it's okay'.

‌



"She said, 'go and live your life for me'. She was so brave, she was our amazing Grace. She doggedly, determinedly fought every single thing. She beat it but in the end the toll was just too many things. She was a gift to the world. She was pure of heart and soul, kind, generous and all the best attributes you could wish to have in a human being.

"The important thing we want to get across is love your kids, you never know when anything could change. And register for stem cell treatment- it's literally a transfusion, it's not an invasive thing and it's almost painless. And blood donation. Grace had so many transfusions. It's a simple thing to do and you save someone's life."

Rather than cards or flowers, the family has asked well-wishers to donate to the wards at the Freeman Hospital, whose devoted care for their daughter they described as "second to none".

Article continues below

Funds raised via the JustGiving page have already reached £7,000, which will go towards the hospital wards and a cancer research charity the family are currently looking into, with the aim of helping others in Grace's situation. The JustGiving page is here.

News.title: Trump sends war threat to Xi as he warns of 'big problem' for China over Iran intervention
News.content:
Trump sends war threat to Xi as he warns of 'big problem' for China over Iran intervention

The US president has sent a fresh threat to China regarding their shipping of arms to Iran in coming weeks as he claims 'regardless what happens, we win' as talks of a deal are held

View 2 Images Trump has sent a fresh warning to China (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

US President Donald Trump has warned China will have “big problems” if it decides to ship arms to Iran.

‌



Trump spoke to reporters on Saturday, April 11 regarding the "very deep negotiations" with Iran.

‌



He sent a direct threat to president Xi warning that China will face a "big problem" if it delivers air defence systems to Iran.

‌



View 2 Images The warning come as Pakistan hold talks (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

It is alleged that the country will send the new systems to Iran within the next few weeks.

When questioned on the matter the US president said: “If China does that, China is gonna have big problems, ok?”

‌



His statement comes as Pakistani officials a hosting face-to-face talks regarding the ceasefire deal with America and Iran.

As the talks are occurring Trump has spoke to media on the White House lawn.

He said that he is "getting a lot of reports: of the negotiations that have been going on for several hours.

‌



Trump added: ""Regardless what happens, we win.

"We've totally defeated that country."

He reiterated that the US has taken out Iran's air force, navy and leadership and is working to open up the Strait of Hormuz, the main condition in the two week ceasefire agreement.

Article continues below

He claimed that the US are working to open the key oil passage on bhalf of other countries who are "afraid or weak or cheap".

"We were not helped by Nato," he told the media.

Referring to the talks held in Pakistan Trump said: "Let's see what happens, but from my standpoint I don't care."

News.title: Britain must 'act today' and prepare for war with Russia, warns General
News.content:
Britain must 'act today' and prepare for war with Russia, warns General

Britain's Armed Forces have been “hollowed out”, Retired General Sir Richard Barrons has said, adding that £10 billion needs to be annually to give the UK the security it needs

View 3 Images A retired British general said the UK needs an extra £10 billion a year to fund its defence (Image: Royal Navy / SWNS)

One of Britain's top retired generals has warned the UK “act today” and prepare for war with Russia.

‌



Retired General Sir Richard Barrons said the country's Armed Forces have been “hollowed out” by cuts and can no longer rely on US support to “bail” Britain out.

‌



He estimates that a yearly increase of £10 billion needs to be found every year so Britain's defence can be properly funded. Sir Richard called this the “bargain of the century” if it ensures Britain never have to pay the huge costs of fighting a war.

‌



“The war in Iran and Russia’s aggression in Europe must be a wake up call for the entire country,” Sir Richard wrote in the Sun. “We must all unite in a national effort to beef up our defences while there is still time, otherwise it could be too late.”

View 3 Images General Sir Richard Barrons (Image: Getty Images)

Ukraine claims Putin’s war funds are running out as Orthodox Easter ceasefire fails READ MORE :

He added: “Russia thinks it is already ‘at war’ with Europe. They hack us, try to meddle in our politics and even hire ‘organised crime’ to sabotage our businesses.

‌



Sir Richard also said the missiles that “rain down” on Ukraine could one day be pointed at Britain.

He said this threat was not “imminent”, but “we need to be ready if the day ever comes”.

The retired general questioned politicians who have failed to fund the military because they “see no votes on it” and that MPs need to “make the hard choices to keep us safe”.

‌



Sir Richard was one of the writers for the government-commission Strategic Defence Review, published last year.

Speaking to BBC Four’s The World At One, he said he had expected it to be enacted through a defence investment plan that took the 62 recommendations and turned them into a 10-year programme of funded activity, but that they are “still waiting for that plan to be issued”.

Sir Richard added that the UK’s armed forces are “grounded in the state the post-Cold War era left them”, but noted that the economic position means the Government is choosing to transform the country’s defence over a period of longer than 10 years, when “you’ve probably got three to five years”.

‌



He argued that it is “not a question of affordability”, but of “hard choices to do without something else to put more money into defence, because it’s vital”.

On the US’s position in NATO, Sir Richard said: “What I think has become more difficult on the back of Greenland and the difficult rhetoric around the war in Iran is the degree of trust between the US and European NATO, and I think that is very dangerous.

“I very badly want to believe that, below the level of rhetoric, substantial things are still holding, and I think they are.”

‌



However, the US cavalry is “not going to come now in the way we’ve become accustomed to since 1949”, he said, which makes the urgency to restore European defences greater, especially if the US exit is “some sort of cliff edge”, rather than managed.

Pressure has mounted on the Government to publish its long-delayed defence investment plan as global tensions simmer following the US-Iran ceasefire.

Defence Secretary John Healey last month denied that the Treasury was holding up the publication of the plan, and rejected suggestions there had been requests to scale it back.

‌



View 3 Images Defence Secretary John Healey said the UK and allies monitored a Russian attack submarine and two spy submarines in the North Atlantic for a month before they retreated (Image: PA)

Labour MP and Commons Defence Committee chairman Tan Dhesi warned its absence risks undermining Britain’s standing in NATO.

Mr Dhesi said the UK’s “inability to deploy a single ship swiftly” after the outbreak of war in the Middle East had left many “embarrassed”.

‌



“The Defence Committee has repeatedly raised concerns around the UK’s lack of mass and capabilities, and the urgent need for investment in UK defence,” he said.

“While the strategic defence review set out the long-term strategic vision for our military, the defence investment plan was meant to provide the details, and its publication has been delayed several months.

“The lack of a public plan now runs the risk of undermining the UK’s ability to play a full and leading role in NATO.”

‌



Real-terms defence spending fluctuated under the successive Conservative governments between 2010 and 2024, falling by 22% by 2016/17, after which it steadily rose and has recently returned to 2010 levels.

Sir Keir’s Labour Government has pledged to spend 2.5% of gross domestic product (GDP) on core defence by 2027, rising to 3% in the next parliament.

Defence minister Luke Pollard accused the Tories of having “hollowed out” the armed forces and “leaving our brave servicemen and women exposed”.

‌



He added: “Prime Minister Keir Starmer is delivering the biggest sustained uplift in defence spending since the end of the Cold War, with every pound of our defence uplift delivering for British workers, British businesses and Britain’s national security.”

Mr Healey, meanwhile, revealed on Thursday that the UK and its allies tracked three Russian vessels off the UK’s northern coast.

A British warship and aircraft were deployed to deter “malign” activity by Vladimir Putin’s regime in waters off the UK’s northern coast, John Healey said.

Article continues below

He said Putin had sought to capitalise on the world being “distracted” by the Iran war and that he poses “the primary threat to UK security”.

News.title: Strait of Hormuz closed 'because Iran misplaced mines in shipping channel', claims US
News.content:
Strait of Hormuz closed 'because Iran misplaced mines in shipping channel', claims US

'Haphazardly' laid mines leaves tankers crossing the Strait of Hormuz vulnerable to being blown up, US officials have said as talks between the US and Iran are underway

View 2 Images The Strait of Hormuz has become a sore point in negotiations between the US and Iran (Image: Getty Images)

The Strait of Hormuz remains closed because Iran "haphazardly" laid mines in the shipping channel, US officials have said.

‌



The Strait is a vital shipping lane for the world’s oil, and was closed by Iran following the outbreak of war with the US and Israel at the end of February. Since then only 12 ships have been allowed to pass through.

‌



But US officials now claim the strait remains closed due to “haphazardly” laid mines leaving tankers vulnerable to being blown up with Iran unable to locate all of the explosives, reports the New York Times.

‌



The US military said two destroyers transited the Strait of Hormuz ahead of mine-clearing work, a first since the war began. However, Iran’s state media earlier said Iran forced a US military ship that was attempting to cross the channel to turn around.

View 2 Images Satellite map shows huge Strait of Hormuz backlog (Image: Marine Traffic)

Iran war peace talks face major gaps between sides in ending conflict READ MORE :

Inside Dubai's hidden crisis as tourists flee and luxury hotspots fall silent READ MORE :

“We’re sweeping the strait. Whether we make a deal or not makes no difference to me,” Mr Trump told journalists as talks continued and the time approached 2am in Islamabad. Iranian state TV noted what it called “serious” differences.

‌



Iran’s chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz has largely cut off the Persian Gulf and its oil and gas exports from the global economy, sending energy prices soaring. Iran's 10-point proposal calls for a guaranteed end to the war and sought control over the Strait of Hormuz. It included ending fighting against Iran's "regional allies," explicitly calling for a halt to Israeli strikes on Hezbollah.

The US and Iran have begun face-to-face negotiations in Pakistan days after a two-week ceasefire was announced, as the war that has killed thousands of people and shaken global markets entered its seventh week.

The White House confirmed the direct nature of the talks. The US delegation led by Vice President JD Vance and the Iranian party led by Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf discussed with Pakistan how to advance the ceasefire already threatened by deep disagreements and Israel’s continued attacks against the Iranian-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon, whose health ministry said the death toll has surpassed 2,000.

‌



Since the Islamic Revolution in Iran in 1979, the most direct US contact had been in 2013 when President Barack Obama called newly elected President Hassan Rouhani to discuss Iran’s nuclear programme. The most recent highest-level meetings were between then secretary of state John Kerry and counterpart Mohammad Javad Zarif during negotiations over the programme.

Now talks feature Mr Vance, a reluctant defender of the war who has little diplomatic experience and warned Iran not to “try and play us”, and Mr Qalibaf, a former commander with Iran’s powerful Revolutionary Guard who has issued some of Iran’s most fiery statements since fighting began.

Iran’s state-run news agency said the three-party talks began after Iranian pre-conditions, including a reduction in Israeli strikes on southern Lebanon, were met.

Article continues below

Iran’s delegation told state television it had presented “red lines” in meetings with Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, including compensation for damage caused by US-Israeli strikes that launched the war on February 28 and releasing Iran’s frozen assets.

The war has killed at least 3,000 people in Iran, 2,020 in Lebanon, 23 in Israel and more than a dozen in Gulf Arab states, and caused lasting damage to infrastructure in half a dozen Middle Eastern countries.

News.title: Wes Streeting warns Nigel Farage can't be trusted with the NHS - 'pack of lies'
News.content:
EXCLUSIVE: Wes Streeting warns Nigel Farage can't be trusted with the NHS - 'pack of lies'

Wes Streeting said Reform pose a far greater threat than the 'wacky' Greens, and warned it represents 'something much, much more dangerous, much more ugly' than Labour's traditional Tory rivals

Streeting warns Farage can't be trusted with the NHS

Nigel Farage can't be trusted with the NHS as he'll sell the country "a pack of lies" again, Wes Streeting has said.

‌



The Health Secretary said Reform pose a far greater threat than the "wacky" Greens, and warned it represents "something much, much more dangerous, much more ugly" than Labour's traditional Tory rivals.

‌



It comes as Labour braces for a tough set of local elections next month, as the party faces pressure on the left and the right.

‌



Mr Streeting has repeatedly seized on Reform's conflicting statements about the NHS, which has seen Mr Farage float the idea of reforms to the funding model. Reform UK said last month: A Reform UK spokesperson said: “We will always keep the NHS free at the point of use for British citizens.”

Wes Streeting 'ashamed' of corridor care as crack teams sent to worst hospitals READ MORE :

View Image Health Secretary Wes Streeting spoke to the Mirror on a visit to Queen's Hospital in Romford. (Image: Philip Coburn/Daily Mirror)

Speaking on a visit to Queen's Hospital, Romford, he said: "The people we've been seeing here in Romford today, these are not people who can afford to pay for their health care. Imagine if they turned up at the A&E department, and people are asking to check their credit card before they get their care. I mean, that's not future the NHS I want to see."

‌



He went on: "There are a lot of traditional Labour people who may be thinking about Reform and thinking, well, maybe that might be my protest vote this time, or maybe that might be something different. And again, I just say, if you care about the NHS, you cannot trust Farage with the NHS.

"He sold this country a pack of lies before and he will do it again. And so we've got to take him on. We've got to beat him. We've got to fight politics as a battle of ideas."

Labour is also facing a threat from an invigorated Green Party, which pulled off an upset in the Gorton and Denton by-election in February. But Mr Streeting dismissed leader Zack Polanski, who suggested hypnosis could increase a woman's breast size while working as a hypnotherapist in 2013.

‌



"I mean that kind of screams oddball, and I don't really know why people are taking the Greens seriously," he said. He also tore into comments from Scottish Green candidate Kate Nevens, who has said she wants to abolish prisons.

He said: "When people look closely at who they are and what they're saying, I'd just say these are not the cuddly conservationist Greens your grandparents voted for."

The Cabinet Minister admitted Labour had made mistakes but said it needs to shout louder about its successes. He said: "I feel proud of what we're doing in Government. We are making a difference. Lots done, so much more to do. Change has begun. The best is still to come."

Article continues below

Mr Streeting, who has long been seen as a possible leadership challenger, said Keir Starmer had shown his mettle over the Iran war.

He said: "What people have seen from Keir Starmer in the context of Iran is the thing that got him elected Prime Minister of this country in the first place - serious level headed leadership, grit and guts, actually.

"I hope that people will give him credit for that, because I think he deserves it, even if he would be too modest to say so himself."

News.title: 'It's a special thing to be on Planet Earth': Artemis crew welcomed home in Houston
News.content:
The four astronauts who flew in Nasa's Artemis II mission around the Moon have been welcomed back to Planet Earth at an event in Houston, Texas.

Commander Reid Wiseman said the mission was "the most special thing I ever went through in my life".

The astronauts - Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, mission specialist Christina Koch and Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen - were all reunited with their families on Saturday.

News.title: Grand National 2026: I Am Maximus becomes two-time winner
News.content:
I Am Maximus became the first horse since Red Rum in 1977 to regain the Grand National as trainer Willie Mullins celebrated his third consecutive victory in the race at Aintree.

The 2024 winner and last year's runner-up came into the race as the 9-2 favourite and backed that up by finishing ahead of Iroko, Jordans and Johnnywho.

It made Irishman Mullins, who won the race for a fourth time in total, the first trainer since Vincent O'Brien between 1953 and 1955 to win in three successive years.

The feat means that JP McManus is now the leading owner in the history of the race with four wins - backing up the victories of Don't Push It in 2010, Minella Times in 2021 and I Am Maximus in 2024.

McManus could also boast owning three of the top four in Saturday's showpiece race, with only Jordans not in his stable.

Red Rum's second and third victories came in 1974 and 1977, and I Am Maximus is the first horse to have won the race in non-consecutive years since.

Further history for I Am Maximus was made by him, with a handicap of 11st 12lbs, becoming the first top weight to win since Red Rum carried 12 stone to victory in 1974.

Jockey Paul Townend said he felt "privileged" to be riding I Am Maximus.

He told ITV: "He's tough. He's a really, really good horse, and although Grangeclare West and Nick Rockett looked good in training, this lad wasn't telling me not to ride him.

"He is so good and has such an engine. He will gallop to the end of the world for you. I am really privileged. What a horse.

"Grand Nationals and Gold Cups are the pinnacle of the sport and I have them both."

Rory McIlroy headed straight to the practice ground range to iron out his problems after surrendering a six-shot lead to leave the defence of his Masters title in the balance.

Twenty-four hours earlier, the Northern Irishman had looked poised to blow the field away after opening up a significant advantage with the biggest 36-hole lead in the tournament’s history.

While all of his rivals were going under par – the nine players immediately below him all shot sub-70 rounds – the world number two could record only a one-over 71 having come unstuck at Amen Corner.

The troubles off the tee which he has been successfully managing all week cost him dearly and he immediately retired to the range to find a fix ahead of his final-group pairing with Cameron Young, who shot a Masters-best 65, on 11 under.

“The course was obviously gettable, there was a lot of good scores out there, and the quality of the chasing pack is obvious,” said McIlroy.

“There’s a lot of guys in with a chance tomorrow. I’m still tied for the best score going into tomorrow, so I can’t forget that, but I do know I’m going to have to be better if I want to have a chance to win.

“I’m in the final group. I just need to go to the range and try to figure it out a little bit.”

McIlroy entered Augusta National’s famously tricky Amen Corner stretch at 13 under, three ahead but clinging on.

He exited it one behind Young after playing it double bogey-bogey-par having pulled a seven iron into the water at the 11th, missing the green at the next and driving into the trees at the 13th.

“When you’re not quite feeling it, you struggle. You have to dig deep and I felt like I did that on the front nine and made a lot of good par saves,” he added.

“I missed a couple of chances on eight and nine and then I thought I turned the round around with the birdie on 10.

“I felt like I hit a pretty good second shot on 11 but it just drifted on the wind a little bit and went in the water. Those two holes (11 and 12) weren’t great.

“But again I felt like I bounced back pretty well with the birdies on 14 and 15. It would have been nice to play those last few holes and not make that bogey on 17 but, you know, I still have a great chance.”

News.title: The Masters LIVE: Rory McIlroy shares lead with Cameron Young after blowing six-shot advantage
News.content:
Rory McIlroy storms to sensational six-shot lead after stunning birdie run at Augusta

Rory McIlroy will go into the final round of the Masters in a share of the lead with Cameron Young after blowing the six-shot advantage he took into the weekend on a dramatic moving day on Saturday.

At -12, McIlroy held an unprecedented lead heading into the third round, as the Northern Irishman bids to become just the fourth man to win the Masters back-to-back, but his healthy position at the top of the leaderboard was wiped out on a wild day at Augusta National.

He will start on -11, along with Players champion Young, after the American caught fire and joined the defending champion at the top just as McIlroy found the water and made a double-bogey-six on the 12th, followed by another bogey on the 13th.

Young’s blazing round of -7 was matched by world No 1 Scottie Scheffler, who will start Sunday four shots behind, with Shane Lowry and last year’s runner-up Justin Rose also in firm contention. Lowry produced the moment of the round with a hole-in-one on the 6th.

Hole-in-one specialist Shane Lowry hailed his “wild” ace at the Masters which helped put him in contention heading into the final day.

The Irishman has quite the collection of ones on his CV and this was his second at Augusta National, becoming the first player to have that honour.

Lowry’s tee shot at the 190-yard sixth saw him jump from six to eight under and he finished nine under after a 69, just two off the lead.

“That’s wild, isn’t it? I made one a couple of weeks ago in Houston. You don’t ever expect to make a hole-in-one, I just couldn’t believe it,” said the former Open champion, whose previous hole-in-one here came at the 16th in the final round of 2016.

“Obviously you’re out there and you’re in the hunt at the Masters and you’re making hole-in-one, it’s pretty cool.

“The walk down the sixth hole with everyone around 16 and the sixth was very special. I’ll remember that for a while. It was obviously amazing.

“It gives you obviously a huge kind of boost. You go from six-under to eight-under and then all of a sudden you’re only four back.

“It’s getting real now. I felt like I did a great job of calming myself down afterwards.”

Lowry has also aced the 17th at Sawgrass, in 2022, and the seventh at Pebble Beach, in January 2025, two of the most famous par threes in golf.

Tyson Fury has claimed he has signed a contract to box Anthony Joshua, but that “AJ” has not done the same.

On Saturday night, Fury emerged from his fifth retirement from boxing, outpointing Arslanbek Makhmudov in Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

And Joshua was sat in the front row, so it was no surprise that he was the subject of a callout from Fury after the latter’s hand was raised.

It was expected that Joshua, 36, would enter the ring to face off with his fellow Briton, 37, but AJ declined to do so, and his response to Fury’s callout was spoiled by a faulty microphone.

Tyson Fury calling out Anthony Joshua after beating Arslanbek Makhmudov ( Getty )

Still, Joshua could be heard suggesting that the Fury fight was not yet a done deal, something that the “Gypsy King” confirmed at the post-fight press conference.

“I’ve signed, done,” Fury claimed. “It doesn’t really matter how many fights it is [on that deal], let’s just get one done.

“He was brought here tonight, ringside, for a reason: to get the fight done. I signed months ago, I don’t know if he’s signed, and by the looks of it, he’s not gonna.

“He didn’t want it, he was shellshocked, he didn’t know what to say. If it was me, I’d have jumped in the ring, faced off, let’s get it on.

President Donald Trump's White House ballroom construction can continue, at least for now.

On Saturday, a federal appeals court ruled that temporary construction on Trump's $400 million ballroom can continue while his administration fights a lower court's ruling that the president's project was beyond the scope of his authority.

A three-judge U.S. circuit court in Washington, D.C., ruled 2-1 that the construction can resume until April 17, when the court revisits the issue, NBC News reports.

The previous court's ruling ordered that construction on the project had to stop by April 14.

Trump has rebuffed attempts to stop the construction of his ballroom by arguing that the “ballroom is clearly a vital project for the safety and security of the White House and the President, his family, and his staff," according to a court document entered by his lawyers.

open image in gallery A U.S. circuit court ruled that construction on President Donald Trump’s ballroom, pictured left, can continue until April 17 after a lower court ruled it had to stop and seek Congressional approval ( The White House )

The appeals court ruling did not offer a ruling on whether or not the "safety and security" issues were legitimate and instructed the original court to review the case and provide clarifications on the matter.

The judge in that case, U.S. District Judge Richard Leon, ruled in favor of a preservation group that opposed the demolition of the White House East Wing and the new ballroom. He determined that Trump had exceeded his authority as president by undertaking the construction and said he needed to seek Congressional approval for the project.

In his initial injunction, Leon noted that the president is the "steward of the White House" but added, "he is not, however, the owner."

Trump's lawyers have argued that there is no need for Congressional approval because the project is reportedly being funded fully through private donations.

“No taxpayer dollars are being used for the funding of this beautiful, desperately needed, and completely secure (for national security purposes) ballroom," they wrote in court documents.

It continued, arguing that other legislative bodies should not have a say in the needs of the president's residence.

open image in gallery The former site of the White House East Wing, which is now an active construction site at work continues on President Donald Trump’s $400 million ballroom project ( Getty Images )

“Congress did not get involved with the design, planning, and architecture of either the original East Wing or the West Wing many decades ago,” the filing said. “Decisions about what is needed to keep the President, his family, and his staff safe rest with the President, and cannot possibly be outsourced to other branches of government, just as the President could not dictate the Senate’s building needs or architectural design.”

Even with private donations, however, the project is still on public ground and makes significant changes to public buildings. The National Trust for Historic Preservation, which opposes the ballroom project, made that argument in an appeal to the ruling. It noted that all construction projects involving federal buildings require congressional approval, while also calling into question the legitimacy of Trump's national security claims.

“Defendants appear to contend that being prevented from illegally constructing a massive ballroom constitutes a national security emergency. It plainly does not,” the NTHP said in the appeal.

The rebuttal also noted that the ballroom will take two years to finish, and that “the absence of a massive ballroom on White House grounds has not stopped this (or any other) President from residing at the White House or hosting events there.”
